post.html:
One of the aspects I like about my job is that I split my time between being an academic researcher and a software engineer. For example, a few years ago, my colleagues and I published a paper on how to use logic programming to recover object-oriented abstractions from an executable. I was very proud of that paper (and still am) because it was both a usable tool (OOAnalyzer) based on some interesting academic ideas.

Although building a tool in Prolog is neat, it can also be challenging. We strugged from the beginning to achieve reasonable performance, and eventually concluded that we had to use tabling in order to achieve reasonable performance. At a high level, tabling is basically memoization for Prolog. Prolog does have side-effects, though, and part of the challenge is making sure that the tables are consistent.

One of the leading Prolog implementations with tabling support is XSB Prolog, which OOAnalyzer has been using since the beginning. XSB and one of its developers, Teri Swift, really helped us get enough performance to be able to write our paper, in which we were able to analyze some real and interesting programs, including a bunch of MySQL utilities. The largest program we were able to test was over 5 MiB.

Unfortunately, there were many programs that we weren't able to test successfully as well. One of these that really stuck in my mind was mysqld.exe. In our paper, we were able to run successfully on mysqld.exe, the MySQL client program, but the daemon was much larger (~22 MiB vs 5 MiB) and always remained elusive.

A while back, we started working with Teri Swift from XSB, who was helping Jan Wielemaker of SWI Prolog add support for tabling to SWI Prolog. Jan graciously helps us get OOAnalyzer running on SWI, which was useful in its own right. He also developed some invaluable debugging tools to understand what tabling is doing behind the scenes. These tools, combined with a lot of profiling and rewriting iterations, eventually allowed us to improve performance bottlenecks to the point that we could successfully handle mysqld.exe. Along the way, we battled performance bottlenecks, memory that would not be reclaimed, and other problems. But now we can analyze mysqld.exe in about 18 hours, and only using about 12 GiB of memory. And what is encouraging is that at the end, the tool is still making new inferences fairly quickly.

Our first completed run showed that we still have work to do. Our accuracy was not so great, and we failed to identify many object oriented methods correctly. But this isn't terribly surprising; this is a program that is much larger and complex than anything we've ever analyzed. So there's bound to be some more work to do.

These updates are available in the latest release of the Pharos repository.
